nodes.name: Generalized Symmetric Space
nodes.statement: Let $G$ be a group and $\theta\in\Aut(G)$ such that $\theta^m={\sf id}$. We then define the following two sets: \begin{align*} H &= G^\theta=\{g\in G\mid \theta(g)=g\}\\ Q &=\{g\in G\mid g=x\theta(x)^{-1} \mbox{ for some } x\in G\}. \end{align*} The set $H$ is the fixed-point subgroup of $\theta$ and $Q$ is known as a {\em Generalized Symmetric Space}.
nodes.statement_short: For $\theta\in\Aut(G)$ of finite order, $H$ is the fixed-point subgroup and $Q=\{x\theta(x)^{-1}\}$ is the generalized symmetric space.

nodes.name: symmetric ${\sf k}$-variety
nodes.statement: If $G$ is a reductive algebraic group defined over an algebraically closed field ${\sf k}$, then $Q$ is also known as a symmetric variety and if $G$ is defined over a non-algebraically closed field ${\sf k}$, then the set $Q_{\sf k}:= \{ x\theta(x)^{-1} \mid x\in G_{\sf k} \}$ is called a symmetric ${\sf k}$-variety. Here $G_{\sf k}$ denotes the set of ${\sf k}$-rational points of $G$.
nodes.statement_short: Over a non-algebraically-closed ${\sf k}$, $Q_{\sf k}=\{x\theta(x)^{-1}\mid x\in G_{\sf k}\}$ is the symmetric ${\sf k}$-variety.
nodes.genus: the set $Q_{\sf k}:= \{ x\theta(x)^{-1} \mid x\in G_{\sf k} \}$

nodes.name: $\theta$-twisted conjugation action
nodes.statement: Both $G$ and $H$ act on $Q$ by $\theta$-twisted conjugation which we denote by $*$. For $g\in G$ and $q\in Q$ we have $$g*q=gq\theta(g)^{-1}.$$ Since $H$ is the set of fixed points, this action is simply conjugation when restricted to $H$.

nodes.name: $Q\cong G/H$ for an involution
nodes.statement: Also, if $\theta$ is an involution, then $Q\cong G/H$ under the map $\tau : G\to Q$ given by $\tau(g)=g\theta(g)^{-1}$.
conclusions: $Q\cong G/H$ under the map $\tau : G\to Q$ given by $\tau(g)=g\theta(g)^{-1}$

nodes.name: $H\backslash Q\cong H\backslash G/H$ for an involution
nodes.statement: In particular, if $\theta$ is an involution it is known that $H\backslash Q\cong H\backslash G/H$.

nodes.name: dihedral group $D_n$
nodes.statement: Throughout the paper we denote by $D_n$ the group of symmetries of the regular $n$-gon. More specifically, $D_n$ is a finitely generated group given by the presentation $$D_n=\langle r,s\mid r^n=s^2=1,\ sr=r^{-1}s\rangle.$$
differentia: given by the presentation $$D_n=\langle r,s\mid r^n=s^2=1,\ sr=r^{-1}s\rangle.$$

nodes.name: normal form of an element of $D_n$
nodes.statement: From the presentation it is clear that \[ D_n = \{ 1, r, r^2, \ldots, r^{n-1}, s, rs, r^2s, \ldots, r^{n-1}s \} \] and we say that an element of $D_n$ is presented in \emph{normal form} if it is written as $r^ks^m$ for some integers $0 \le k < n$ and $s \in \{0, 1\}$.
differentia: it is written as $r^ks^m$ for some integers $0 \le k < n$ and $s \in \{0, 1\}$

nodes.name: $\Z_n$ and the unit group $U_n$
nodes.statement: Throughout the paper, $\Z_n$ denotes the additive group of integers modulo $n$ and $U_n$ denotes the multiplicative group of units of $\Z_n$. Recall that $a \in U_n$ if and only if $(\dot{a},n) = 1$ for any representative integer $\dot{a}$ of $a \in \Z_n$.
nodes.genus: the multiplicative group of units of $\Z_n$

nodes.name: $k$-th roots of unity $\mathcal{R}_n^k$ in $\Z_n$
nodes.statement: We also find it useful to have terminology for the $k$-th roots of unity in $\Z_n$ (equivalently in $U_n$), which can be described by $$\mathcal{R}_n^k:=\{a\in U_n\mid a^k=1\}.$$
nodes.genus: the $k$-th roots of unity in $\Z_n$ (equivalently in $U_n$)

nodes.name: Lemma 1.1 ($\Aut(D_n)\cong\Aff(\Z_n)$)
nodes.statement: The automorphism group of $D_n$ is isomorphic to the group of affine linear transformations of $\Z_n$: $$\Aut(D_n)\cong \Aff(\Z_n)=\left\{ ax+b: \Z_n\to\Z_n \mid a \in U_n, b \in \Z_n \right\}$$ and the action of $ax+b$ on elements of $D_n$ in normal form is given by: \[ (ax+b).(r^k s^m) = r^{ak+bm}s^m.\]
nodes.statement_short: $\Aut(D_n)$ is the affine group $\Aff(\Z_n)$, with $ax+b$ acting by $(ax+b).(r^ks^m)=r^{ak+bm}s^m$.
assumptions: Throughout the paper we denote by $D_n$ the group of symmetries of the regular $n$-gon.
conclusions: The automorphism group of $D_n$ is isomorphic to the group of affine linear transformations of $\Z_n$: $$\Aut(D_n)\cong \Aff(\Z_n)=\left\{ ax+b: \Z_n\to\Z_n \mid a \in U_n, b \in \Z_n \right\}$$
the action of $ax+b$ on elements of $D_n$ in normal form is given by: \[ (ax+b).(r^k s^m) = r^{ak+bm}s^m.\]

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 1.1
nodes.statement: Observe that $\theta(r)$ must have order $n$ since $r$ does. The elements of $D_n$ of order $n$ are precisely the $\{ r^a \mid a \in U_n \}$. So let $\theta(r) = r^a$ for some $a$ relatively prime to $n$. Similarly, $\theta(s)=r^bs$ for some $0 \le b < n$ since $s$ has order 2 and the only elements of $D_n$ of order 2 are of the form $r^bs$. Putting these together, we see that if $\theta\in\Aut(D_n)$, then for any $r^ks^m\in D_n$ we must have $\theta(r^ks^m)=r^{ak+bm}s^m$. There is now a clear map from $\Aut(D_n)\to \Aff(\Z_n)$ and it is easily checked to be an isomorphism.
nodes.statement_short: Determine the images of the generators $r$ and $s$ from their orders, then check the induced map to $\Aff(\Z_n)$ is an isomorphism.

nodes.name: Example 1.2 (inner automorphisms of $D_n$)
nodes.statement: Consider $\theta = \autconj(g)$, conjugation by an element $g\in D_n$. If $\theta = ax + b$ from Lemma \ref{lem:aut}, and if $g=r^k$, then it is easy to see that $a=1$ and $b=2k$ (in $U_n$ and $\Z_n$ respectively). Also, if $g=r^ks$, then we have $a=n-1$ and $b=2k$. In particular, if $\theta=ax+b$ is an \emph{inner automorphism}, then (abusing notation) we have $a\equiv\pm 1 \pmod{n}$. Also, we see that when $n$ is even, there are $n$ distinct inner automorphisms (corresponding to $a\equiv\pm 1\pmod{n}$ and $b\in\langle2\rangle\leq \Z_n$, and when $n$ is odd, there are $2n$ distinct inner automorphisms corresponding to $a\equiv\pm 1\pmod{n}$ and $b\in\langle2\rangle=\Z_n$. Finally, note that the identity automorphism of $D_n$ corresponds to $x \in \Aff(\Z_n)$.
nodes.statement_short: Conjugation by $r^k$ gives $a=1,b=2k$ and by $r^ks$ gives $a=n-1,b=2k$; so inner automorphisms have $a\equiv\pm1$.

nodes.name: Example 1.3 (diagram automorphism of $D_n$)
nodes.statement: It is well known from the theory of Coxeter groups that when $n$ is even, there is an outer automorphism of $D_n$ corresponding to the interchanging of the two conjugacy classes of reflections, also known as the diagram automorphism (cf. \cite[\S4.2]{Bourbaki}). This automorphism is described by $\theta=ax+b$ where $a=n-1$ and $b=n-1$. The previous example shows that this automorphism is inner when $n$ is odd, and outer when $n$ is even.
nodes.statement_short: The Coxeter diagram automorphism is $\theta=(n-1)x+(n-1)$; it is inner for odd $n$ and outer for even $n$.

nodes.name: Notational convention $\theta=ax+b$
nodes.statement: Throughout the paper we abuse notation and write $\theta = ax+b$ for elements $\theta \in \Aut(D_n)$ according to Lemma \ref{lem:aut}.

nodes.name: $\zdiv{c}$, the annihilator of $c$ in $\Z_n$
nodes.statement: For any $c\in\Z_n$, we define $\zdiv{c}=\{y\in\Z_n\mid cy\equiv 0 \mbox{ mod } n\}$.

nodes.name: $\zdiv{c}$ is a subgroup of order $\gcd(c,n)$
nodes.statement: It is trivial to check that $\zdiv{c}$ is a subgroup of $\Z_n$. In particular, $\zdiv{c}=\ker\pi_{c}$ where $\pi_{c}:\Z_n\to\Z_n$ given by $\pi_{c}(x)=cx$. Note that $\im(\pi_{c})=\langle c\rangle$ and so $|\im(\pi_{c})|=\frac{n}{\gcd(c,n)}$. Since $\im(\pi_{c})\cong \Z_n/\ker(\pi_{c})\cong \Z_n/\zdiv{c}$, it follows that $|\zdiv{c}|=\gcd(c,n)$.
nodes.statement_short: $\zdiv{c}=\ker\pi_c$ is a subgroup of $\Z_n$ of order $\gcd(c,n)$.

nodes.name: Proposition 2.1 (automorphisms with $\theta^k={\sf id}$)
nodes.statement: Let $k\geq 1$ be an integer and $\theta\in\Aut(D_n)$ with $\theta=ax+b$. Then $\theta^k={\sf id}$ if and only if $a\in\mathcal{R}_n^k$ and $b\in \zdiv{a^{k-1}+a^{k-2}+\cdots +a+1}$.
nodes.statement_short: $\theta=ax+b$ satisfies $\theta^k={\sf id}$ exactly when $a$ is a $k$-th root of unity and $b$ is annihilated by $a^{k-1}+\cdots+1$.
assumptions: Let $k\geq 1$ be an integer and $\theta\in\Aut(D_n)$ with $\theta=ax+b$.
conclusions: $\theta^k={\sf id}$ if and only if $a\in\mathcal{R}_n^k$ and $b\in \zdiv{a^{k-1}+a^{k-2}+\cdots +a+1}$.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 2.1
nodes.statement: Straightforward computation in $\Aut(D_n)$ gives us that $$\theta^k=a^kx+(a^{k-1}+a^{k-2}+\cdots +a+1)b$$ Since we have identified the identity automorphism with $x \in \Aff(\Z_n)$ the following two equations hold: \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} a^k & \equiv 1 \pmod{n} \\ (a^{k-1} + a^{k-2} + \cdots + 1) b & \equiv 0 \pmod{n}. \end{aligned} \end{equation} In the notation described above, these are evidently equivalent to $a\in\mathcal{R}_n^k$ and\\ $b\in~\zdiv{a^{k-1}+a^{k-2}+\cdots +a+1}$.
nodes.statement_short: Compute $\theta^k$ explicitly and translate the two resulting congruences into the $\mathcal{R}_n^k$ / $\zdiv{\cdot}$ notation.

nodes.name: Order-$k$ congruences (2.1)
nodes.statement: \begin{aligned} a^k & \equiv 1 \pmod{n} \\ (a^{k-1} + a^{k-2} + \cdots + 1) b & \equiv 0 \pmod{n}. \end{aligned}
nodes.statement_short: The congruences equivalent to $\theta^k={\sf id}$ for $\theta=ax+b$.

nodes.name: $\Aut_k(D_n)$
nodes.statement: In what follows, we let $\Aut_k(D_n)=\{\theta\in\Aut(D_n) \mid \theta^k={\sf id}\}\subseteq \Aut(D_n)$.

nodes.name: Proposition 2.2 (counting $|\Aut_k(D_n)|$)
nodes.statement: For any $n$ and $k\geq 1$, we have $$|\Aut_k(D_n)|=\sum_{a\in \mathcal{R}_n^k}\gcd(a^{k-1}+a^{k-2}+\cdots+a+1,n).$$
nodes.statement_short: $|\Aut_k(D_n)|$ is the sum over $k$-th roots of unity $a$ of $\gcd(a^{k-1}+\cdots+a+1,n)$.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 2.2
nodes.statement: This follows from Proposition \ref{prop:orderk}: for any $a\in\mathcal{R}_n^k$ there are $$\abs{\zdiv{a^{k-1}+a^{k-2}+\cdots+1}}=\gcd(a^{k-1}+a^{k-2}+\cdots+1,n)$$ elements $b$ such that $(a^{k-1}+a^{k-2}+\cdots+1)b\equiv 0$ (mod $n$), and every automorphism $\theta\in\Aut_k(D_n)$ must be of this form.
nodes.statement_short: Sum the number of admissible $b$ over each admissible $a$, using $|\zdiv{c}|=\gcd(c,n)$.

nodes.name: Definition 2.3 (equivalent automorphisms)
nodes.statement: Let $\theta_1, \theta_2\in\Aut(D_n)$. We say that $\theta_1$ is \textit{equivalent} to $\theta_2$ and write $\theta_1\sim\theta_2$ if and only if they are conjugate to each other, i.e. if there is $\sigma\in\Aut(D_n)$ with $\sigma\theta_1\sigma^{-1}=\theta_2$. For any $\theta\in\Aut(D_n)$ we let $\overline{\theta}=\{\sigma\in\Aut(D_n)\mid \theta\sim \sigma\}$ be the equivalence class of $\theta$.

nodes.name: Remark 2.4 (breadth of the equivalence)
nodes.statement: This definition of equivalence is broad (since we allow conjugation by any automorphism, not just the inner ones), but still useful. In particular, it simplifies the statement of the following proposition and it allows us not to worry about the parity of $n$ in several places.

nodes.name: Proposition 2.5 (criterion for $\theta_1\sim\theta_2$)
nodes.statement: Let $\theta_1=ax+b\in\Aut(D_n)$ and $\theta_2=cx+d\in\Aut(D_n)$. Then $\theta_1\sim\theta_2$ if and only if $a=c$ and $fb-d\in\langle a-1\rangle\leq \Z_n$ for some $f\in U_n$.
nodes.statement_short: Two automorphisms are equivalent iff their leading coefficients agree and their constant terms differ by $\langle a-1\rangle$ up to a unit.
conclusions: $\theta_1\sim\theta_2$ if and only if $a=c$ and $fb-d\in\langle a-1\rangle\leq \Z_n$ for some $f\in U_n$.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 2.5
nodes.statement: Suppose that $\sigma=fx+g\in\Aut(D_n)$ (so that $f\in U_n$ and $g\in\Z_n$). It is easily checked that $\sigma^{-1}=f^{-1}x-f^{-1}g$ where $f^{-1}\in\Z_n$ since $f\in U_n$. Then $\sigma\theta_1\sigma^{-1}=\tau$, where $\tau=f(a(f^{-1}x-f^{-1}g)+b)+g=ax+fb-g(a-1)$. Thus, we can conclude that $\sigma\theta_1\sigma^{-1}=\theta_2$ if and only if $a=c$ and $fb-g(a-1)= d$. The second equation can be written as $fb-d=g(a-1)$, and thus $fb-d\in\langle a-1\rangle$.
nodes.statement_short: Conjugate $\theta_1$ by a general $\sigma=fx+g$ and read off when the result equals $\theta_2$.

nodes.name: Proposition 2.6 (equivalence classes indexed by $(a,B)$)
nodes.statement: Suppose $n$ is fixed and let $k\geq 1$. \begin{enumerate} \item For any $a\in\mathcal{R}_n^k$, $\langle a-1\rangle\leq \zdiv{a^{k-1}+a^{k-2}+\cdots+a+1}$. \item For any $a\in\mathcal{R}_n^k$, $U_n$ acts on the cosets $\zdiv{a^{k-1}+a^{k-2}+\cdots+a+1}/\langle a-1\rangle$. \item The set $\Aut_k(D_n)$ is partitioned into equivalence classes indexed by pairs $(a,B)$ where $a\in\mathcal{R}_n^k$ and $B$ is an orbit of $U_n$ on \hbox{$\zdiv{a^{k-1}+a^{k-2}+\cdots +a+1}/\langle a-1\rangle$}. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: $\Aut_k(D_n)$ splits into classes indexed by a $k$-th root of unity $a$ together with a $U_n$-orbit on $\zdiv{a^{k-1}+\cdots+1}/\langle a-1\rangle$.
conclusions: For any $a\in\mathcal{R}_n^k$, $U_n$ acts on the cosets $\zdiv{a^{k-1}+a^{k-2}+\cdots+a+1}/\langle a-1\rangle$.

The set $\Aut_k(D_n)$ is partitioned into equivalence classes indexed by pairs $(a,B)$ where $a\in\mathcal{R}_n^k$ and $B$ is an orbit of $U_n$ on \hbox{$\zdiv{a^{k-1}+a^{k-2}+\cdots +a+1}/\langle a-1\rangle$}.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 2.6
nodes.statement: Part (1) is trivial since $(a-1)(a^{k-1}+a^{k-2}+\cdots +a+1)=a^k-1\equiv 0$. For part (2), we simply recognize that $U_n=\Aut(\Z_n)$ acts on $\Z_n$ by multiplication and since every subgroup is cyclic, $U_n$ must stabilize the subgroups of $\Z_n$. Finally, part (3) is simply Proposition \ref{prop:equivalence} in terms of the $U_n$-action on $\zdiv{a^{k-1}+a^{k-2}+\cdots +a+1}/\langle a-1\rangle$.
nodes.statement_short: Three short parts: a divisibility identity, stability of subgroups under $U_n$, and a restatement of Proposition 2.5.

nodes.name: $N_a$, the number of classes with leading coefficient $a$
nodes.statement: For fixed $a\in\mathcal{R}_n^k$, we want to compute \begin{equation} N_a:=|\{\overline{\theta}\mid \theta=ax+b\in\Aut_k(D_n)\}|. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Theorem 2.7 (number of $U_n$-orbits)
nodes.statement: Let $n$ be fixed and let $a\in\mathcal{R}_n^k$. Then, the number of orbits of $U_n$ on $\zdiv{a^{k-1}+a^{k-2}+\cdots +a+1}/\langle a-1\rangle$ is equal to the number of divisors of $$\frac{\gcd(a-1,n)\gcd(a^{k-1}+a^{k-2}+\cdots+a+1,n)}{n}.$$
nodes.statement_short: The number of $U_n$-orbits on $\zdiv{a^{k-1}+\cdots+1}/\langle a-1\rangle$ equals the number of divisors of $\gcd(a-1,n)\gcd(a^{k-1}+\cdots+1,n)/n$.
conclusions: the number of orbits of $U_n$ on $\zdiv{a^{k-1}+a^{k-2}+\cdots +a+1}/\langle a-1\rangle$ is equal to the number of divisors of $$\frac{\gcd(a-1,n)\gcd(a^{k-1}+a^{k-2}+\cdots+a+1,n)}{n}.$$

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2.7
nodes.statement: The $U_n$-orbits on $\Z_n$ are indexed by the subgroups of $\Z_n$. Thus, the $U_n$-orbits on $\zdiv{a^{k-1}+a^{k-2}+\cdots +a+1}/\langle a-1\rangle$ are indexed by subgroups $L\leq \Z_n$ such that $\langle a-1\rangle\leq L\leq \zdiv{a^{k-1}+a^{k-2}+\cdots +a+1}$. It is well known that the subgroup lattice of $\Z_n$ is isomorphic to the divisor lattice of $n$. Under the previous lattice isomorphism, the subgroup $\langle a-1\rangle$ corresponds to the divisor $\gcd(a-1,n)$ and the subgroup $\zdiv{a^{k-1}+a^{k-2}+\cdots +a+1}$ corresponds to the divisor $$\frac{n}{\gcd(a^{k-1}+\cdots+a+1,n)},$$ and the subgroups between these groups correspond to the divisors of $n$ between $\gcd(a-1,n)$ and $\frac{n}{\gcd(a^{k-1}+\cdots+a+a,n)}$ in the divisor lattice. Finally, it is known that this sub-lattice of the divisors of $n$ is isomorphic to the divisor lattice of $$\frac{\gcd(a-1,n)}{\frac{n}{\gcd(a^{k-1}+\cdots+a+1,n)}}=\frac{\gcd(a-1,n)\gcd(a^{k-1}+a^{k-2}+\cdots+a+1,n)}{n}.$$
nodes.statement_short: Transport the orbit count through the isomorphism between the subgroup lattice of $\Z_n$ and the divisor lattice of $n$.

nodes.name: Theorem 3.1 (description of $H$ and $Q$ for $D_n$)
nodes.statement: Let $G=D_n$ and $\theta=ax+b\in\Aut(D_n)$ be of finite order, and let $H$ and $Q$ be as defined above. Then $$ \begin{aligned} H&=\{r^k\mid k(a-1)\equiv 0 \mbox{ (mod $n$)}\}\cup \{r^ks\mid k(a-1)\equiv -b \mbox{ (mod $n$)}\}\ \mbox{and}\\ Q&=\{r^k\mid k\in\langle a-1\rangle\cup(-b+\langle a-1\rangle)\}. \end{aligned} $$
nodes.section: 3 Fixed Groups and Symmetric Spaces of Automorphisms
nodes.statement_short: For $\theta=ax+b$ of finite order, $H$ consists of the $r^k$ with $k(a-1)\equiv0$ together with the $r^ks$ with $k(a-1)\equiv-b$, and $Q=\{r^k\mid k\in\langle a-1\rangle\cup(-b+\langle a-1\rangle)\}$.
assumptions: Let $G=D_n$ and $\theta=ax+b\in\Aut(D_n)$ be of finite order, and let $H$ and $Q$ be as defined above.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3.1
nodes.statement: Recall that if $\theta=ax+b\in\Aut(D_n)$, then the formula $\theta(r^ks^m)=r^{ak+bm}s^m$ provides the full description of the action of $\theta$. All of the results of the theorem arise from the definitions of $H$ and $Q$ using the action described above by $\theta$. We demonstrate the computation for $H$ in what follows, and $Q$ is similar. Suppose $\theta(r^k)=r^k$, then $r^{ak}=r^k$ and so $ak-k\equiv 0$ (mod $n$), i.e. $k(a-1)\equiv 0$ (mod $n$). On the other hand, if $\theta(r^ks)=r^ks$, then $r^{ak+b}s=r^ks$ and so $ak-k+b\equiv 0$ (mod $n$), i.e. $k(a-1)\equiv -b$ (mod $n$).
nodes.section: 3 Fixed Groups and Symmetric Spaces of Automorphisms
nodes.statement_short: Apply the explicit action $\theta(r^ks^m)=r^{ak+bm}s^m$ to the two normal-form cases $r^k$ and $r^ks$.

nodes.name: Corollary 3.2 (structure of $H$)
nodes.statement: Let $\theta=ax+b\in\Aut(D_n)$ be of finite order. Then \begin{enumerate} \item If $b\not\in\langle a-1\rangle$, then $H\cong\zdiv{a-1}$ is cyclic. \item If $b\in\langle a-1\rangle$, then $H\cong\zdiv{a-1} \rtimes \Z_2$ is dihedral. \end{enumerate}
nodes.section: 3 Fixed Groups and Symmetric Spaces of Automorphisms
nodes.statement_short: $H$ is cyclic $\cong\zdiv{a-1}$ when $b\notin\langle a-1\rangle$ and dihedral $\cong\zdiv{a-1}\rtimes\Z_2$ otherwise.

nodes.name: Corollary 3.3 ($Q$ is a subgroup when $b\in\langle a-1\rangle$)
nodes.statement: Let $n$, $k$, and $\theta=ax+b\in\Aut_k(D_n)$ be fixed. If $b\in\langle a-1\rangle$ then $Q$ is a subgroup of $D_n$ and $Q\cong\langle a-1\rangle$.
nodes.section: 3 Fixed Groups and Symmetric Spaces of Automorphisms
conclusions: $Q$ is a subgroup of $D_n$ and $Q\cong\langle a-1\rangle$.

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 3.3
nodes.statement: Since $b\in\langle a-1\rangle$, then it follows from Theorem \ref{thm:hqr} that $Q=\{r^k\mid k\in\langle a-1\rangle\}$.
nodes.section: 3 Fixed Groups and Symmetric Spaces of Automorphisms
nodes.statement_short: The two cosets in Theorem 3.1 collapse to $\langle a-1\rangle$ when $b\in\langle a-1\rangle$.

nodes.name: Corollary 3.4 (when $HQ=D_n$)
nodes.statement: Let $\theta=ax+b\in\Aut(D_n)$ be a fixed automorphism. If $b\not\in\langle a-1\rangle$, then $HQ\ne D_n$. If $b\in\langle a-1\rangle$, then the following are equivalent \begin{enumerate} \item $HQ=D_n$ \item $H\cap Q=\{1\}$ in $D_n$, and \item $\gcd(a-1,n)$ is relatively prime to $\frac{n}{\gcd(a-1,n)}$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.section: 3 Fixed Groups and Symmetric Spaces of Automorphisms
nodes.statement_short: $HQ=D_n$ can only happen when $b\in\langle a-1\rangle$, and then it is equivalent to $H\cap Q=\{1\}$ and to a coprimality condition on $\gcd(a-1,n)$.

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 3.4
nodes.statement: From Corollary \ref{h-structure} and the fact that $Q\subseteq\langle r\rangle$, we see that if $b\not\in\langle a-1\rangle$ then $HQ \subseteq\langle r\rangle\ne D_n$. If $b\in\langle a-1\rangle$ then $H$ contains a reflection and so $HQ = D_n$ if and only if $r\in HQ$. From Corollaries \ref{h-structure} and \ref{cor:qgroup}, we see that $r\in HQ$ if and only if the subgroups $\zdiv{a-1}$ and $\langle a-1\rangle$ in $\Z_n$ have relatively prime generators. This last condition is clearly equivalent to both (2) and (3).

nodes.statement_short: Split on whether $H$ contains a reflection, then reduce $r\in HQ$ to coprimality of the generators of $\zdiv{a-1}$ and $\langle a-1\rangle$.

nodes.name: Example 3.5 (three automorphisms of $D_{36}$)
nodes.statement: Let $G=D_{36}$. We illustrate Theorem \ref{thm:hqr} and its corollaries for three different automorphisms of $D_{36}$. First, consider the automorphism $\theta_1=19x+18$. Note that $\theta_1$ is an involution. Applying Theorem \ref{thm:hqr} yields that for $\theta_1$, $H=H_1=\{1,r^2,r^4,\ldots,r^{34}, r^3s,r^5s,\ldots, r^{35}s\}$ and $Q=Q_1=\{1,r^ {18}\}$, which gives that $H_1\cap Q_1=\{1,r^{18}\}=Q_1$. Observe that the statement of Corollary \ref{cor:qgroup} holds in this case: $H_1 Q_1\neq D_{36}$. This follows from the fact that $18\in\langle 18\rangle$, but $\gcd(18,36)=18$ is not relatively prime to $36/\gcd(18,36)=2$. Now consider $\theta_2=5x+2$ which is an automorphism of order 6. In this case, $H_2=\{1,r^9,r^{18},r^{27}\}$ and $Q_2= \{1,r^2,r^4,\ldots,r^{34}\}$. Thus, $H_2\cap Q_2=\{1, r^{18}\}$ and $H_2 Q_2=D_{36}$. However, in this case it is because $2\not\in \langle 4\rangle$. Finally, consider the automorphism $\theta_3 = 5x + 4$ of $D_{36}$. This is also an automorphism of order 6. In this case, $H_3 = \{1, r^9, r^{18}, r^{27}, r^8s, r^{17}s, r^{26}s, r^{35}s\}$ and $Q_3 = \{1, r^4, r^8, r^{12}, \ldots , r^{32}\}$. Thus, $H_3 \cap Q_3 = \{1\}$ and this agrees with Corollary \ref{cor:qgroup} since $r^9r^{28} = r$ and so $H_3 Q_3 = D_{36}$.

nodes.statement_short: Worked computation of $H$, $Q$ and $HQ$ for $\theta_1=19x+18$, $\theta_2=5x+2$ and $\theta_3=5x+4$ in $D_{36}$.

nodes.name: Proposition 3.6 ($H$-orbits and $G$-orbits on $Q$)
nodes.statement: Let $G=D_n$ and $\theta=ax+b\in\Aut_k(D_n)$ for some $k$. \begin{enumerate} \item If $b\not\in\langle a-1\rangle$, then the $H$-orbits on $Q$ are: $$H\backslash Q=\left\{\{r^j\}\mid j\in \langle a-1\rangle\cup(-b+\langle a-1\rangle)\right\}.$$ \item If $b\in\langle a-1\rangle$, then the $H$-orbits on $Q$ are: $$H\backslash Q=\left\{\{r^j, r^{-j}\}\mid j\in \langle a-1\rangle\right\}.$$ \end{enumerate} In either situation $G\backslash Q=\{Q\}$, i.e. there is a single $G$-orbit on $Q$.
nodes.section: 3 Fixed Groups and Symmetric Spaces of Automorphisms
nodes.statement_short: The $H$-orbits on $Q$ are singletons when $b\notin\langle a-1\rangle$ and pairs $\{r^j,r^{-j}\}$ otherwise, while $G$ acts transitively on $Q$.
conclusions: If $b\not\in\langle a-1\rangle$, then the $H$-orbits on $Q$ are: $$H\backslash Q=\left\{\{r^j\}\mid j\in \langle a-1\rangle\cup(-b+\langle a-1\rangle)\right\}.$$
If $b\in\langle a-1\rangle$, then the $H$-orbits on $Q$ are: $$H\backslash Q=\left\{\{r^j, r^{-j}\}\mid j\in \langle a-1\rangle\right\}.$$
In either situation $G\backslash Q=\{Q\}$, i.e. there is a single $G$-orbit on $Q$.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 3.6
nodes.statement: Since $H$ is fixed by $\theta$, the action of $H$ on $Q$ is simply by conjugation. We note that $Q\subseteq \langle r\rangle\leq D_n$ and so we only need to describe the action of $H$ on a general element, $r^j$. Then, let $r^i\in\{r^k\mid k(a-1)\equiv 0 \pmod{n}\} \subseteq H$. We see $r^ir^jr^{-i}=r^j$ so $\langle r\rangle$ fixes $Q$ pointwise. Now suppose $r^is\in\{r^ks\mid k(a-1)\equiv -b \pmod{n}\}\subseteq H$. We have $r^isr^j(r^is)^{-1}=r^{-j}$ and so $r^is$ takes $r^j$ to $r^{-j}$. The result now follows since we will have $\{r^j,r^{-j}\}$ as an orbit if and only if there is $r^is\in H$, which is true if and only if $b\in\langle a-1\rangle$. Finally, we demonstrate that every element of $Q$ is in the $G$-orbit of $1\in Q$. Notice that every element of $Q$ is either of the form $q_1=r^{p(a-1)}\in Q$ or $q_2=r^{-b+p(a-1)}\in Q$. We have $r^{-p}\in G$ and $r^{-p}1\theta(r^{-p})^{-1}=r^{p(a-1)}=q_1$. Additionally, we have $r^{-p}s\in G$ and $r^{-p}s1\theta(r^{-p}s)^{-1}=r^{-p}r^{ap-b}=r^{-b+p(a-1)}=q_2$. Therefore, for any $q\in Q $, we can find $g\in G$ such that $g1\theta(g)^{-1}=q$ and so $G*1=Q$. Hence $G\backslash Q=\{Q\}$.
nodes.section: 3 Fixed Groups and Symmetric Spaces of Automorphisms
nodes.statement_short: Conjugating $r^j$ by rotations fixes it and by reflections inverts it; then exhibit a $g$ with $g*1=q$ for each $q\in Q$.

nodes.name: Example 3.7 ($H$-orbits for the three automorphisms of $D_{36}$)
nodes.statement: Revisiting $\theta_1$, $\theta_2$, and $\theta_3$ of Example \ref{autexamples}, we apply Proposition \ref{orbits} to obtain that for $\theta_1$, since $18\in \langle 18\rangle$ and $r^{18} = r^{-18} \in D_{36}$, $$H_1\backslash Q_1=\{\{1\},\{r^{18}\}\};$$ for $ \theta_2$, since $2\not\in\langle 4\rangle$, $$H_2\backslash Q_2=\{\{1\},\{r^2\},\{r^4\},\ldots,\{r^{34}\}\};$$ lastly, for $ \theta_3$, since $4\in\langle 4\rangle$, $$H_3\backslash Q_3 = \{\{1\}, \{r^4,r^{-4}\}, \{r^8,r^{-8}\}, \ldots, \{r^{32},r^{-32}\}\}. $$

nodes.statement_short: The $H$-orbit decompositions of $Q$ for $\theta_1,\theta_2,\theta_3$ of Example 3.5.

nodes.name: Theorem 4.1 (number of square roots of unity $|\mathcal{R}_n^2|$)
nodes.statement: Suppose that $n\geq 1$ and $n=2^mp_1^{r_1}\cdots p_k^{r_k}$ where the $p_i$ are distinct odd primes. Then, $$|\mathcal{R}_n^2|=\begin{cases} 2^k & \mbox{ if $m=0,1$}\\ 2^{k+1} & \mbox{ if $m=2$}\\ 2^{k+2} & \mbox{ if $m\geq 3$}. \end{cases}$$
nodes.statement_short: $|\mathcal{R}_n^2|$ is $2^k$, $2^{k+1}$ or $2^{k+2}$ according as the $2$-part of $n$ has exponent $m\le1$, $m=2$ or $m\ge3$.
assumptions: Suppose that $n\geq 1$ and $n=2^mp_1^{r_1}\cdots p_k^{r_k}$ where the $p_i$ are distinct odd primes.

nodes.name: Remark 4.2 (constructive computation of square roots of unity)
nodes.statement: We include the proof of Theorem \ref{thm:squareroots1} in Appendix \ref{sec:appendix} because it demonstrates exactly how to construct the square roots of unity in $\Z_n$ provided we have the prime factorization of $n$. The construction only involves the Euclidean Algorithm and a map provided by the Chinese Remainder Theorem. One can use the procedure described in the proof to effectively compute the square roots of unity in $\Z_n$ for any $n$. The construction of the square roots of unity provided in the appendix also provides the understanding necessary for Corollary \ref{cor:equivclassformula} below.
nodes.statement_short: The appendix proof of Theorem 4.1 is constructive: Euclid's algorithm plus the Chinese Remainder Theorem produce all square roots of unity in $\Z_n$.

nodes.name: Corollary 4.3 (number of involutions $|\Aut_2(D_n)|$)
nodes.statement: For any $n \ge 1$, $$|\Aut_2(D_n)|=\sum_{a\in \mathcal{R}_n^2}\gcd(a+1,n).$$

nodes.name: Remark 4.4 (computing and plotting the number of involutions)
nodes.statement: Corollary \ref{cor:numinvols} together with the proof of Theorem \ref{thm:squareroots1} (see Remark \ref{rmk:computesqr}) gives an easy way to compute the total number of involutions in $\Aut(D_n)$. Figure \ref{fig:numinvolutions} provides a graph of the number of involutions in $D_n$ for $n\leq 200$. This plot was generated using Sage \cite{sage}.

nodes.name: Theorem 4.5 (equivalence classes of involutions, $N_a\le2$)
nodes.statement: Let $a\in\mathcal{R}_n^2$. The following hold. \begin{enumerate} \item $\langle a-1\rangle\leq \zdiv{a+1}$ and $|\zdiv{a+1}/\langle a-1\rangle|\leq 2$. \item $N_a = \left| \zdiv{a+1}/\langle a-1 \rangle \right| \leq 2 $. \item $N_a=2$ if and only if $n=2^m\cdot k$ where $k\geq1$ is odd, $m > 0$, and \hbox{$a \equiv \pm 1 \pmod{2^m}$.} \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: For an involution parameter $a$, $\langle a-1\rangle\le\zdiv{a+1}$ with index at most $2$, so $N_a\le2$, with $N_a=2$ exactly when $a\equiv\pm1\pmod{2^m}$.
conclusions: $N_a=2$ if and only if $n=2^m\cdot k$ where $k\geq1$ is odd, $m > 0$, and \hbox{$a \equiv \pm 1 \pmod{2^m}$.}

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4.5
nodes.statement: The first part of (1) is simply a restatement of Proposition \ref{lem:equivalence} part (1). Now, suppose that $|\zdiv{a+1}/\langle a-1\rangle|=j$. It is well known that $|\langle a-1\rangle|=\frac{n}{\gcd(a-1,n)}$ and we have already observed that $|\zdiv{a+1}|=\gcd(a+1,n)$. Thus we have that $\frac{\gcd(a+1,n)}{\frac{n}{\gcd(a-1,n)}}=j$, or $\gcd(a+1,n)\gcd(a-1,n)=jn$. Now, suppose that $$n=2^mp_1^{r_1}\cdots p_k^{r_k}$$ with $m\geq 0$, the $p_i$ distinct odd primes, and $r_i\geq 1$. Then, we must have that \begin{itemize} \item[] $\gcd(a+1,n)=2^{m'}p_1^{s_1}\cdots p_k^{s_k}$ with $m'\leq m$ and $0\leq s_i\leq r_i$ for all $i$, and \item[] $\gcd(a-1,n)=2^{m''}p_1^{t_1}\cdots p_k^{t_k}$ with $m''\leq m$ and $0\leq t_i\leq r_i$ for all $i$. \end{itemize} Now, we note that for all $i\in\{1,...,k\}$ either $s_i=0$ or $t_i=0$. Indeed, if $s_i>0$ and $t_i>0$ then $p_i$ divides both $a-1$ and $a+1$ which is impossible (since $p_i>2$). Similarly, either $m'\leq1$ or $m''\leq1$; otherwise, $2^{\min\{m',m''\}}$ divides $a-1$ and $a+1$ which is impossible. Since $\gcd(a+1,n)\gcd(a-1,n)=jn$, we have that $$2^{m'+m''}p_1^{s_1+t_1}\cdots p_k^{s_k+t_k}=j2^mp_1^{r_1}\cdots p_k^{r_k}.$$ Now, since for all $i$ either $t_i=0$ or $s_i=0$, we necessarily have $s_i+t_i=r_i$. Dividing out, we get $2^{m'+m''}=j2^m$. We also know that $m'\leq m$ and $m''\leq m$ and since either $m'\leq 1$ or $m''\leq 1$, we have $m\leq m'+m''\leq m+1$. Dividing out we have $j=2^{m'+m''-m}$ and so $1\leq j\leq 2$ as required. Now, according to Theorem \ref{unorbits}, $N_a$ is the number of divisors of $\frac{\gcd(a-1,n)\gcd(a+1,n)}{n}$, and thus $N_a$ is the number of divisors of $j$ computed above. Therefore, $N_a=1$ if $j=1$ and $N_a=2$ if $j=2$. In either case, $N_a = |\zdiv{a+1}/\langle a-1 \rangle| \le 2$ proving Claim (2). Finally, according to the proof of (1), we have $j=2$ if and only if $m'=1$ and $m''=m$ or $m'=m$ and $m''=1$. In the first case, we have that $2^m$ divides $a-1$, and in the second case we have that $2^m$ divides $a+1$. Therefore, $a \equiv \pm 1 \pmod{2^m}$.
nodes.statement_short: Write $\gcd(a+1,n)\gcd(a-1,n)=jn$ and use that $a-1$ and $a+1$ share no odd prime and at most one factor $2$ to force $j\in\{1,2\}$.

nodes.name: Corollary 4.6 (closed formula for the number $C_n$ of classes)
nodes.statement: Suppose that $n\geq 1$ and $n=2^mp_1^{r_1}\cdots p_k^{r_k}$ where the $p_i$ are distinct odd primes. Then, the number of equivalence classes, $C_n$, of $\Aut_2(D_n)$ is given by $$C_n=\begin{cases} 2^k & \mbox{ if $m=0$}\\ 2^{k+1} & \mbox{ if $m=1$}\\ 2^{k+2} & \mbox{ if $m=2$}\\ 2^{k+3}-2^{k+1} & \mbox{ if $m\geq 3$}. \end{cases}$$
nodes.statement_short: The number of equivalence classes of $\Aut_2(D_n)$ is $2^k,2^{k+1},2^{k+2}$ or $2^{k+3}-2^{k+1}$ according to the $2$-adic valuation $m$ of $n$.
assumptions: Suppose that $n\geq 1$ and $n=2^mp_1^{r_1}\cdots p_k^{r_k}$ where the $p_i$ are distinct odd primes.
conclusions: the number of equivalence classes, $C_n$, of $\Aut_2(D_n)$ is given by $$C_n=\begin{cases} 2^k & \mbox{ if $m=0$}\\ 2^{k+1} & \mbox{ if $m=1$}\\ 2^{k+2} & \mbox{ if $m=2$}\\ 2^{k+3}-2^{k+1} & \mbox{ if $m\geq 3$}. \end{cases}$$

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 4.6
nodes.statement: According to Theorem \ref{thm:equivinvols}, we know $N_a$ for every $a\in\mathcal{R}_n^2$. When $m=0$, $n$ is odd and we know that $N_a=1$ for all $a$. Thus, there is one equivalence class for every element of $\mathcal{R}_n^2$ proving the first formula. If $m=1,2$, then every $a\in\mathcal{R}_n^2$ is odd and so satisfies $a\equiv \pm 1\pmod{m}$. Thus for every element $a\in\mathcal{R}_n^2$, we get two equivalence classes for a total of $2\cdot|\mathcal{R}_n^2|$ equivalence classes. Finally, when $m\geq 3$, using the construction of the elements of $\mathcal{R}_n^2$ found in the proof in the appendix, we see that exactly half of these elements satisfy the condition $a\equiv\pm 1\pmod{m}$. Therefore, for half the elements in $\mathcal{R}_n^2$ we have $N_a=1$ and for the other half we have $N_a=2$ giving us a total of $2^{k+2}+(2^{k+2}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot2^{k+2})=2^{k+3}-2^{k+1}$ equivalence classes, proving the result.
nodes.statement_short: Add up $N_a$ over $a\in\mathcal{R}_n^2$, splitting on $m=0$, $m=1,2$ and $m\ge3$ (where exactly half the $a$ have $N_a=2$).

nodes.name: Remark 4.7 (OEIS A147848 and the group-extension bijection)
nodes.statement: According to the Online Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences, the sequence described in Corollary \ref{cor:equivclassformula} also counts the number (up to isomorphism) of groups of order $2n$ that have a subgroup isomorphic to $\mathbb Z_n$ \cite{oeisA147848}. To be more precise, we include a brief discussion of the natural bijection between these two objects. Suppose $\theta=ax+b$ is an involution. Then $w_a:\Z_2\to\Aut(\Z_n)=U_n$ given by $w_a(0)=1$ and $w_a(1)=-a$ is an injective homomorphism and induces a $\Z_2$-action on $\Z_n$. Next, we define $f:\Z_2\times\Z_2\to\Z_n$ by $f(c,d)=0$ if $c=0$ or $d=0$ and $f(1,1)=b$; it is easily shown that $f$ is a 2-cocycle if and only if $b\in\zdiv{a+1}$. Finally, it is well known (see \cite[Chapter 6.6]{weibel})) that 2-cocyles give rise to group extensions and two different 2-cocycles give isomorphic group extensions if they are cohomologous. A simple calculation shows that if $\theta=ax+b$ and $\theta'=ax+b'$, then the corresponding 2-cocycles are cohomologous if and only if $b-b'\in\langle a-1\rangle$, which matches the characterization of automorphisms being equivalent above.
nodes.statement_short: The sequence $C_n$ also counts groups of order $2n$ containing $\Z_n$, via the bijection between involutions and $2$-cocycles up to cohomology.

nodes.name: twisted involutions $R$
nodes.statement: moreover, in this situation, we are also interested in the set of twisted involutions $$R=R_\theta=\{x\in G\mid \theta(x)=x^{-1}\}.$$

nodes.name: Explicit description of $R$ for an involution (4.2)
nodes.statement: If $\theta=ax+b$ is an involution, a quick calculation gives \begin{equation} R=\{r^k\mid k\in\zdiv{a+1}\}\cup \{r^ks\mid k(a-1)\equiv -b\pmod{n}\}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: For an involution, $R$ consists of the $r^k$ with $k\in\zdiv{a+1}$ together with the $r^ks$ with $k(a-1)\equiv-b$.

nodes.name: Corollary 4.8 ($Q$ is a subgroup; description of $R\setminus Q$)
nodes.statement: If $\theta=ax+b$ is an involution, then $Q$ is a subgroup of $\langle r \rangle$ and under the natural isomorphism $\psi: \langle r \rangle \buildrel\cong\over\longrightarrow \Z_n$ we have \[ \psi(Q) = \begin{cases} \langle a-1 \rangle, & \text{if} \quad b \in \langle a-1 \rangle \\ \zdiv{a+1}, & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases} \] Furthermore, $R \setminus Q = \{r^k\mid k\in\zdiv{a+1}\setminus\langle a-1\rangle\}\cup\{r^ks \mid k(a-1)\equiv -b\pmod{n}\}$
nodes.statement_short: For an involution, $\psi(Q)$ is $\langle a-1\rangle$ if $b\in\langle a-1\rangle$ and $\zdiv{a+1}$ otherwise; in particular $Q\le\langle r\rangle$.
conclusions: $Q$ is a subgroup of $\langle r \rangle$ and under the natural isomorphism $\psi: \langle r \rangle \buildrel\cong\over\longrightarrow \Z_n$ we have \[ \psi(Q) = \begin{cases} \langle a-1 \rangle, & \text{if} \quad b \in \langle a-1 \rangle \\ \zdiv{a+1}, & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases} \]

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 4.8
nodes.statement: We proceed using Theorem \ref{thm:hqr} and applying Theorem \ref{thm:equivinvols}. Indeed, by Theorem \ref{thm:hqr} $\psi(Q)$ consists of the union of the two cosets $\langle a-1 \rangle$ and $-b + \langle a-1 \rangle$. These cosets are the same if $-b \in \langle a-1 \rangle$ (which means $b\in\langle a-1\rangle$) and then $\psi(Q) = \langle a - 1 \rangle \le \zdiv{a+1}$, or they are distinct and by Theorem \ref{thm:equivinvols} part (1) there are only 2 cosets total so $\langle a - 1 \rangle \cup (-b+\langle a - 1 \rangle) = \zdiv{a+1}$. In either case, $Q$ is a subgroup of $\langle r \rangle$ and $\psi(Q)$ is as described in the statement of the corollary. Finally, the result about $R \setminus Q$ is immediate from equation \eqref{eqn:R}.
nodes.statement_short: The two cosets of Theorem 3.1 either coincide or, by Theorem 4.5(1), exhaust $\zdiv{a+1}$; either way $\psi(Q)$ is a subgroup.

nodes.name: Corollary 4.9 ($R=Q$ when $b\not\in\langle a-1\rangle$)
nodes.statement: If $b\not\in\langle a-1\rangle$ then $R=Q$.

nodes.name: Remark 4.10 ($\psi(Q)$ is almost always $\zdiv{a+1}$)
nodes.statement: We note that due to Theorem \ref{thm:equivinvols}, $\psi(Q)$ given in Corollary \ref{cor:Q-is-ZDiv} is almost always $\zdiv{a+1}$ for involutions. The only instance where $\psi(Q)\ne \zdiv{a+1}$ occurs when $|\zdiv{a+1}/\langle a-1 \rangle|=2$ and $b\in\langle a-1\rangle$. We revisit $\theta_1=19x+18$ from Example \ref{autexamples}, which is an involution, noting that this is in fact a case where $b\in\langle a-1\rangle$. Recalling that $Q_1=\{1,r^{18}\}$, we see that $\psi (Q_1)$ is indeed isomorphic to $\langle a-1\rangle=\langle 18\rangle < \mathbb Z_{36}$. We also have that $R=R_1=\{1,r,r^3,r^5,\dots,r^{17},r^{18},r^{19},r^{21},\dots, r^{35}\}$, and thus $R_1\setminus Q_1=\{r,r^3,r^5,\dots,r^{35}\}$.
nodes.statement_short: $\psi(Q)\ne\zdiv{a+1}$ only when the index is $2$ and $b\in\langle a-1\rangle$, as illustrated by $\theta_1=19x+18$ in $D_{36}$.

nodes.name: Contrast with algebraic groups: $Q$ is always a subgroup here
nodes.statement: Corollary \ref{cor:Q-is-ZDiv} is interesting because in the setting of algebraic groups, the symmetric space $Q$ is almost never a subgroup; whereas here $Q$ is always a subgroup.

nodes.name: Equivalence of involutions in algebraic groups ($\theta_1\sim\theta_2 \iff H_{\theta_1}\cong H_{\theta_2}$)
nodes.statement: In the setting of algebraic groups, it is known that involutions $\theta_1 \sim \theta_2$ if and only if $H_{\theta_1}\cong H_{\theta_2}$ (see \cite{Helm-Wang93}).
nodes.statement_short: For algebraic groups, two involutions are equivalent exactly when their fixed-point groups are isomorphic.
assumptions: In the setting of algebraic groups
conclusions: involutions $\theta_1 \sim \theta_2$ if and only if $H_{\theta_1}\cong H_{\theta_2}$

nodes.name: Corollary 4.11 (counterexample: $H_{\theta_1}=H_{\theta_2}$ but $\theta_1\not\sim\theta_2$)
nodes.statement: There exists $n$ and involutions $\theta_1,\theta_2\in\Aut(D_n)$ such that $H_{\theta_1} = H_{\theta_2}$ but $\theta_1 \not\sim \theta_2$.
nodes.statement_short: The algebraic-group criterion fails for finite dihedral groups: some inequivalent involutions share the same fixed group.
conclusions: There exists $n$ and involutions $\theta_1,\theta_2\in\Aut(D_n)$ such that $H_{\theta_1} = H_{\theta_2}$ but $\theta_1 \not\sim \theta_2$.

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 4.11
nodes.statement: Let $n=8$ and $\theta_1=7x$ and $\theta_2=3x$. According to Proposition \ref{prop:equivalence}, $\theta_1\not\sim\theta_2$ because $7 \ne 3$ (in $U_8$). However, according to Theorem \ref{thm:hqr}, $H_{\theta_1}=\{1, r^4, s, r^4s\}$ and $H_{\theta_2}=\{1, r^4, s, r^4s\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Exhibit $n=8$, $\theta_1=7x$, $\theta_2=3x$: inequivalent by Proposition 2.5 yet with identical fixed groups by Theorem 3.1.

nodes.name: infinite dihedral group $D_\infty$
nodes.statement: However, it turns out that there are similar results for the infinite dihedral group \[ D_\infty=\langle r,s\mid s^2=1,\ rs=sr^{-1}\rangle. \]

nodes.name: Automorphisms of $D_\infty$ of finite order
nodes.statement: In this case, the automorphisms are the affine linear transformations of $\Z$, so are of the form $ax+b$ where $b\in\Z$ and $a\in\{\pm 1\}$. Then, the congruences given in equation \eqref{congruences} become equations over the integers. In particular, it easy to show that the only automorphisms of finite order, besides the identity, are the involutions and they have the form $-x+b$ where $b\in\Z$.
nodes.statement_short: $\Aut(D_\infty)$ consists of the maps $ax+b$ with $a=\pm1$, and the only finite-order ones besides the identity are the involutions $-x+b$.
conclusions: the automorphisms are the affine linear transformations of $\Z$, so are of the form $ax+b$ where $b\in\Z$ and $a\in\{\pm 1\}$
the only automorphisms of finite order, besides the identity, are the involutions and they have the form $-x+b$ where $b\in\Z$

nodes.name: Proposition 5.1 (finite-order automorphisms of $D_\infty$ and their classes)
nodes.statement: The following hold: \begin{enumerate} \item If $\theta \in \Aut(D_\infty)$ has finite order, then $\theta = -x + b$ for some integer $b$. \item $-x + b \sim -x + d$ if and only if $b \equiv d \pmod{2}$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Every finite-order $\theta\in\Aut(D_\infty)$ is $-x+b$, and $-x+b\sim-x+d$ iff $b\equiv d\pmod 2$.
conclusions: $-x + b \sim -x + d$ if and only if $b \equiv d \pmod{2}$

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 5.1
nodes.statement: Part (1) follows from the equations \eqref{congruences} given in the proof of Proposition \ref{prop:orderk}. For part (2), observe that Proposition \ref{prop:equivalence} holds for $D_\infty$ and says that $-x + b \sim -x + d$ if and only if either $b - d \in 2\Z$ or $-b-d \in 2\Z$, equivalently: $b \equiv d \pmod{2}$.
nodes.statement_short: Part (1) from the order congruences over $\Z$; part (2) from Proposition 2.5 applied to $D_\infty$.

nodes.name: the involution classes $\chi_0$ and $\chi_1$ of $D_\infty$
nodes.statement: We see that in $D_\infty$ the situation is simple: the only automorphisms of finite order are involutions and there are only two distinct equivalence classes of involutions represented by $\chi_0 = -x = \autconj(s)$ (inner) and $\chi_1 = -x+1$ (outer).

nodes.name: Fixed groups and symmetric spaces of $\chi_0,\chi_1$ (5.1)
nodes.statement: The fixed group and symmetric space of an involution $\theta = \chi_i$ is similarly easy to compute. \begin{equation} \begin{array}{lll} H_{\chi_0} = \{1, s\},& Q_{\chi_0} = \langle r^2 \rangle,& R_{\chi_0} = \langle r^2 \rangle \cup \{ s \} \\ H_{\chi_1} = \{ 1 \}, & Q_{\chi_1} = \langle r \rangle,& R_{\chi_1} = \langle r \rangle. \end{array} \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: $H_{\chi_0}=\{1,s\}$, $Q_{\chi_0}=\langle r^2\rangle$, while $H_{\chi_1}=\{1\}$ and $Q_{\chi_1}=R_{\chi_1}=\langle r\rangle$.
assumptions: The fixed group and symmetric space of an involution $\theta = \chi_i$
conclusions: H_{\chi_0} = \{1, s\},& Q_{\chi_0} = \langle r^2 \rangle,& R_{\chi_0} = \langle r^2 \rangle \cup \{ s \}

nodes.name: Corollary 4.8 in the infinite case
nodes.statement: We note that the descriptions in equation \eqref{eq:hqr-infty} show that Corollary \ref{cor:Q-is-ZDiv} holds in the infinite case as well. However, in this case, the description is simpler because the description of $Q$ depends only on whether $b$ is even or odd. We also note that despite the fact that the two cases are different when viewing $Q$ as a subgroup of $D_\infty$, we always have $Q\cong \Z$.
nodes.statement_short: Equation (5.1) confirms Corollary 4.8 for $D_\infty$, where $Q$ depends only on the parity of $b$ and is always $\cong\Z$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4.1 (appendix)
nodes.statement: Our goal is to determine the size of $|\mathcal{R}_n^2|$ for all $n$. First, suppose that $n=p^r$ where $p$ is an odd prime and $r\geq 1$. Then, suppose $a\in\Z_{p^r}$ and that $a^2-1\equiv 0\pmod{p^r}$. Then we have that $(a+1)(a-1)\equiv 0$ (mod $p^r$) and so $(a+1)(a-1)=kp^r$ for some $k\in\Z$. Since $p$ is an odd prime, it is clear that both $a+1$ and $a-1$ cannot divide $p^d$ for any $d\geq 1$ and so we have that $a+1=p^r$ or $a-1=p^r$. This implies that $a=1$ or $a=n-1$, thus $|\mathcal{R}_{p^r}^2|=2$. Next, it is clear that $|\mathcal{R}_2^2|=1$ and $|\mathcal{R}_4^2|=2$. Suppose that $n=2^m$ with $m\geq 3$. Next, suppose that $a\in\Z_n\setminus\{1,n-1\}$ with $a^2\equiv 1$ (mod $n$). Since $n$ is even, we must have that $a$ is odd, so assume that $a=2k+1$ for some $0\leq k\leq 2^{m-1}$. Then $1\equiv a^2\equiv (2k+1)^2\equiv 4k^2+4k+1$ (mod $n$) so that $4k(k+1)=l\cdot 2^m$ for some $l\geq 1$. In particular, since $m\geq 3$, we have $k(k+1)=l\cdot 2^{m-2}$ for some $m$. Either $k$ or $k+1$ is odd and thus cannot divide $2^{m-2}$. \begin{enumerate} \item[] Case 1: $k$ is even. So $k=h\cdot 2^{m-2}$ for some $1\leq h\leq 2$ (since $k\leq 2^{m-1})$. Then, if $h=1$, $a=2^{m-1}+1$. If $h=2$, then $a\equiv 1$ (mod $n$). \item[] Case 2: $k$ is odd. So $k+1$ is even and $k+1=h\cdot 2^{m-2}$ with $1\leq h\leq 2$. Then, if $h=1$, $a=2^{m-1}-1$. If $h=2$, then $a=2^m-1\equiv n-1\equiv -1$ (mod $n$). \end{enumerate} So, there are four possibilities for $a$: $1,-1,2^{m-1}+1,2^{m-1}-1$. It is easy to check that these are all in fact square roots of 1, showing that $|\mathcal{R}_{2^m}^2|=4$ if $m\geq 3$. Finally, the result holds due to the fact that the Chinese Remainder Theorem guarantees that if $n=2^mp_1^{r_1}\cdots p_k^{r_k}$ then $$\Z_n\cong \Z_{2^m}\times\Z_{p_1^{r_1}}\times\cdots\times \Z_{p_k^{r_k}}.$$ Then, it is clear that any square root of $(1,...,1)$ (the identity from the right hand side) must be of the form $(a_0,a_1,...,a_k)$ where $a_0\in\mathcal{R}_{2^m}^2$ and $a_i\in\mathcal{R}_{p_i^{r_i}}^n$ for $i\in\{1,...,k\}$. We have counted the possibilities for $a_i$ above and so we can multiply these together to get all the possible choices for $a\in\Z_n$ with $a^2\equiv 1$ (mod $n$). In particular, we get $|\mathcal{R}_n^2|=2^k$ if $m\in\{0,1\}$, $|\mathcal{R}_n^2|=2\cdot2^k$ if $m=2$ and $|\mathcal{R}_n^2|=2^2\cdot2^k$ if $m\geq 3$ as required.
nodes.statement_short: Case analysis on odd prime powers and on $2^m$ (via $4k(k+1)\equiv0$), then recombine with the Chinese Remainder Theorem.

nodes.name: Order of $\theta(r)$
nodes.statement: Observe that $\theta(r)$ must have order $n$ since $r$ does. The elements of $D_n$ of order $n$ are precisely the $\{ r^a \mid a \in U_n \}$.
nodes.statement_short: Note $\theta(r)$ has order $n$, so lies among the $r^a$ with $a\in U_n$.

nodes.name: Images of the generators
nodes.statement: So let $\theta(r) = r^a$ for some $a$ relatively prime to $n$. Similarly, $\theta(s)=r^bs$ for some $0 \le b < n$ since $s$ has order 2 and the only elements of $D_n$ of order 2 are of the form $r^bs$.
nodes.statement_short: Introduce $\theta(r)=r^a$ and $\theta(s)=r^bs$ using the orders of $r$ and $s$.

nodes.name: General formula for $\theta$
nodes.statement: Putting these together, we see that if $\theta\in\Aut(D_n)$, then for any $r^ks^m\in D_n$ we must have $\theta(r^ks^m)=r^{ak+bm}s^m$.
nodes.statement_short: Combine to get $\theta(r^ks^m)=r^{ak+bm}s^m$.

nodes.name: Isomorphism onto $\Aff(\Z_n)$
nodes.statement: There is now a clear map from $\Aut(D_n)\to \Aff(\Z_n)$ and it is easily checked to be an isomorphism.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude the induced map $\Aut(D_n)\to\Aff(\Z_n)$ is an isomorphism.

nodes.name: Compute $\theta^k$
nodes.statement: Straightforward computation in $\Aut(D_n)$ gives us that $$\theta^k=a^kx+(a^{k-1}+a^{k-2}+\cdots +a+1)b$$
nodes.statement_short: Expand $\theta^k=a^kx+(a^{k-1}+\cdots+1)b$.

nodes.name: Equate with the identity
nodes.statement: Since we have identified the identity automorphism with $x \in \Aff(\Z_n)$ the following two equations hold: \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} a^k & \equiv 1 \pmod{n} \\ (a^{k-1} + a^{k-2} + \cdots + 1) b & \equiv 0 \pmod{n}. \end{aligned} \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Setting $\theta^k={\sf id}$ yields the two congruences (2.1).

nodes.name: Translate into $\mathcal{R}_n^k$ and $\zdiv{\cdot}$
nodes.statement: In the notation described above, these are evidently equivalent to $a\in\mathcal{R}_n^k$ and\\ $b\in~\zdiv{a^{k-1}+a^{k-2}+\cdots +a+1}$.
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite the congruences as $a\in\mathcal{R}_n^k$ and $b\in\zdiv{a^{k-1}+\cdots+1}$.

nodes.name: General conjugator and its inverse
nodes.statement: Suppose that $\sigma=fx+g\in\Aut(D_n)$ (so that $f\in U_n$ and $g\in\Z_n$). It is easily checked that $\sigma^{-1}=f^{-1}x-f^{-1}g$ where $f^{-1}\in\Z_n$ since $f\in U_n$.
nodes.statement_short: Take $\sigma=fx+g$ and compute $\sigma^{-1}=f^{-1}x-f^{-1}g$.

nodes.name: Compute the conjugate
nodes.statement: Then $\sigma\theta_1\sigma^{-1}=\tau$, where $\tau=f(a(f^{-1}x-f^{-1}g)+b)+g=ax+fb-g(a-1)$.
nodes.statement_short: Compute $\sigma\theta_1\sigma^{-1}=ax+fb-g(a-1)$.

nodes.name: Conditions for equality with $\theta_2$
nodes.statement: Thus, we can conclude that $\sigma\theta_1\sigma^{-1}=\theta_2$ if and only if $a=c$ and $fb-g(a-1)= d$.
nodes.statement_short: Equality with $\theta_2$ forces $a=c$ and $fb-g(a-1)=d$.

nodes.name: Rewrite as a coset condition
nodes.statement: The second equation can be written as $fb-d=g(a-1)$, and thus $fb-d\in\langle a-1\rangle$.
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite the second condition as $fb-d\in\langle a-1\rangle$.

nodes.name: Part (1)
nodes.statement: Part (1) is trivial since $(a-1)(a^{k-1}+a^{k-2}+\cdots +a+1)=a^k-1\equiv 0$.
nodes.statement_short: The identity $(a-1)(a^{k-1}+\cdots+1)=a^k-1\equiv0$ gives the containment.

nodes.name: Part (2)
nodes.statement: For part (2), we simply recognize that $U_n=\Aut(\Z_n)$ acts on $\Z_n$ by multiplication and since every subgroup is cyclic, $U_n$ must stabilize the subgroups of $\Z_n$.
nodes.statement_short: $U_n=\Aut(\Z_n)$ stabilizes every subgroup of the cyclic group $\Z_n$, so the action descends.

nodes.name: Part (3)
nodes.statement: Finally, part (3) is simply Proposition \ref{prop:equivalence} in terms of the $U_n$-action on $\zdiv{a^{k-1}+a^{k-2}+\cdots +a+1}/\langle a-1\rangle$.
nodes.statement_short: Part (3) is Proposition 2.5 restated in terms of the $U_n$-action.

nodes.name: Orbits indexed by intermediate subgroups
nodes.statement: The $U_n$-orbits on $\Z_n$ are indexed by the subgroups of $\Z_n$. Thus, the $U_n$-orbits on $\zdiv{a^{k-1}+a^{k-2}+\cdots +a+1}/\langle a-1\rangle$ are indexed by subgroups $L\leq \Z_n$ such that $\langle a-1\rangle\leq L\leq \zdiv{a^{k-1}+a^{k-2}+\cdots +a+1}$.
nodes.statement_short: $U_n$-orbits correspond to subgroups $L$ with $\langle a-1\rangle\le L\le\zdiv{a^{k-1}+\cdots+1}$.

nodes.name: Pass to the divisor lattice
nodes.statement: It is well known that the subgroup lattice of $\Z_n$ is isomorphic to the divisor lattice of $n$. Under the previous lattice isomorphism, the subgroup $\langle a-1\rangle$ corresponds to the divisor $\gcd(a-1,n)$ and the subgroup $\zdiv{a^{k-1}+a^{k-2}+\cdots +a+1}$ corresponds to the divisor $$\frac{n}{\gcd(a^{k-1}+\cdots+a+1,n)},$$ and the subgroups between these groups correspond to the divisors of $n$ between $\gcd(a-1,n)$ and $\frac{n}{\gcd(a^{k-1}+\cdots+a+a,n)}$ in the divisor lattice.
nodes.statement_short: Translate the two bounding subgroups into their corresponding divisors of $n$.

nodes.name: Count the divisors
nodes.statement: Finally, it is known that this sub-lattice of the divisors of $n$ is isomorphic to the divisor lattice of $$\frac{\gcd(a-1,n)}{\frac{n}{\gcd(a^{k-1}+\cdots+a+1,n)}}=\frac{\gcd(a-1,n)\gcd(a^{k-1}+a^{k-2}+\cdots+a+1,n)}{n}.$$
nodes.statement_short: The interval of the divisor lattice is the divisor lattice of $\gcd(a-1,n)\gcd(a^{k-1}+\cdots+1,n)/n$.

nodes.name: Recall the action of $\theta$
nodes.statement: Recall that if $\theta=ax+b\in\Aut(D_n)$, then the formula $\theta(r^ks^m)=r^{ak+bm}s^m$ provides the full description of the action of $\theta$. All of the results of the theorem arise from the definitions of $H$ and $Q$ using the action described above by $\theta$. We demonstrate the computation for $H$ in what follows, and $Q$ is similar.
nodes.section: 3 Fixed Groups and Symmetric Spaces of Automorphisms
nodes.statement_short: Recall $\theta(r^ks^m)=r^{ak+bm}s^m$ and reduce to computing $H$.

nodes.name: Rotations fixed by $\theta$
nodes.statement: Suppose $\theta(r^k)=r^k$, then $r^{ak}=r^k$ and so $ak-k\equiv 0$ (mod $n$), i.e. $k(a-1)\equiv 0$ (mod $n$).
nodes.section: 3 Fixed Groups and Symmetric Spaces of Automorphisms
nodes.statement_short: $\theta(r^k)=r^k$ is equivalent to $k(a-1)\equiv0 \pmod n$.

nodes.name: Reflections fixed by $\theta$
nodes.statement: On the other hand, if $\theta(r^ks)=r^ks$, then $r^{ak+b}s=r^ks$ and so $ak-k+b\equiv 0$ (mod $n$), i.e. $k(a-1)\equiv -b$ (mod $n$).
nodes.section: 3 Fixed Groups and Symmetric Spaces of Automorphisms
nodes.statement_short: $\theta(r^ks)=r^ks$ is equivalent to $k(a-1)\equiv-b \pmod n$.

nodes.name: Case $b\not\in\langle a-1\rangle$
nodes.statement: From Corollary \ref{h-structure} and the fact that $Q\subseteq\langle r\rangle$, we see that if $b\not\in\langle a-1\rangle$ then $HQ \subseteq\langle r\rangle\ne D_n$.
nodes.section: 3 Fixed Groups and Symmetric Spaces of Automorphisms
nodes.statement_short: If $b\notin\langle a-1\rangle$ then $HQ$ sits inside $\langle r\rangle$, so $HQ\ne D_n$.

nodes.name: Case $b\in\langle a-1\rangle$
nodes.statement: If $b\in\langle a-1\rangle$ then $H$ contains a reflection and so $HQ = D_n$ if and only if $r\in HQ$.
nodes.section: 3 Fixed Groups and Symmetric Spaces of Automorphisms
nodes.statement_short: If $H$ contains a reflection then $HQ=D_n$ reduces to $r\in HQ$.

nodes.name: Coprimality criterion
nodes.statement: From Corollaries \ref{h-structure} and \ref{cor:qgroup}, we see that $r\in HQ$ if and only if the subgroups $\zdiv{a-1}$ and $\langle a-1\rangle$ in $\Z_n$ have relatively prime generators. This last condition is clearly equivalent to both (2) and (3).
nodes.section: 3 Fixed Groups and Symmetric Spaces of Automorphisms
nodes.statement_short: $r\in HQ$ iff the generators of $\zdiv{a-1}$ and $\langle a-1\rangle$ are coprime, which is (2) and (3).

nodes.name: Reduce to conjugation on $\langle r\rangle$
nodes.statement: Since $H$ is fixed by $\theta$, the action of $H$ on $Q$ is simply by conjugation. We note that $Q\subseteq \langle r\rangle\leq D_n$ and so we only need to describe the action of $H$ on a general element, $r^j$.
nodes.section: 3 Fixed Groups and Symmetric Spaces of Automorphisms
nodes.statement_short: The $H$-action on $Q\subseteq\langle r\rangle$ is ordinary conjugation of $r^j$.

nodes.name: Rotations act trivially
nodes.statement: Then, let $r^i\in\{r^k\mid k(a-1)\equiv 0 \pmod{n}\} \subseteq H$. We see $r^ir^jr^{-i}=r^j$ so $\langle r\rangle$ fixes $Q$ pointwise.
nodes.section: 3 Fixed Groups and Symmetric Spaces of Automorphisms
nodes.statement_short: Rotations in $H$ fix every $r^j$.

nodes.name: Reflections invert
nodes.statement: Now suppose $r^is\in\{r^ks\mid k(a-1)\equiv -b \pmod{n}\}\subseteq H$. We have $r^isr^j(r^is)^{-1}=r^{-j}$ and so $r^is$ takes $r^j$ to $r^{-j}$. The result now follows since we will have $\{r^j,r^{-j}\}$ as an orbit if and only if there is $r^is\in H$, which is true if and only if $b\in\langle a-1\rangle$.
nodes.section: 3 Fixed Groups and Symmetric Spaces of Automorphisms
nodes.statement_short: A reflection $r^is\in H$ sends $r^j\mapsto r^{-j}$, and exists iff $b\in\langle a-1\rangle$.

nodes.name: Single $G$-orbit
nodes.statement: Finally, we demonstrate that every element of $Q$ is in the $G$-orbit of $1\in Q$. Notice that every element of $Q$ is either of the form $q_1=r^{p(a-1)}\in Q$ or $q_2=r^{-b+p(a-1)}\in Q$. We have $r^{-p}\in G$ and $r^{-p}1\theta(r^{-p})^{-1}=r^{p(a-1)}=q_1$. Additionally, we have $r^{-p}s\in G$ and $r^{-p}s1\theta(r^{-p}s)^{-1}=r^{-p}r^{ap-b}=r^{-b+p(a-1)}=q_2$. Therefore, for any $q\in Q $, we can find $g\in G$ such that $g1\theta(g)^{-1}=q$ and so $G*1=Q$. Hence $G\backslash Q=\{Q\}$.
nodes.section: 3 Fixed Groups and Symmetric Spaces of Automorphisms
nodes.statement_short: Exhibit $g$ with $g*1=q$ for each $q\in Q$, so $G\backslash Q=\{Q\}$.

nodes.name: Part (1), containment
nodes.statement: The first part of (1) is simply a restatement of Proposition \ref{lem:equivalence} part (1).
nodes.statement_short: The containment $\langle a-1\rangle\le\zdiv{a+1}$ is Proposition 2.6(1).

nodes.name: Set the index $j$
nodes.statement: Now, suppose that $|\zdiv{a+1}/\langle a-1\rangle|=j$. It is well known that $|\langle a-1\rangle|=\frac{n}{\gcd(a-1,n)}$ and we have already observed that $|\zdiv{a+1}|=\gcd(a+1,n)$. Thus we have that $\frac{\gcd(a+1,n)}{\frac{n}{\gcd(a-1,n)}}=j$, or $\gcd(a+1,n)\gcd(a-1,n)=jn$.
nodes.statement_short: Write the index as $j$ and derive $\gcd(a+1,n)\gcd(a-1,n)=jn$.

nodes.name: Factor $n$ and the two gcds
nodes.statement: Now, suppose that $$n=2^mp_1^{r_1}\cdots p_k^{r_k}$$ with $m\geq 0$, the $p_i$ distinct odd primes, and $r_i\geq 1$. Then, we must have that \begin{itemize} \item[] $\gcd(a+1,n)=2^{m'}p_1^{s_1}\cdots p_k^{s_k}$ with $m'\leq m$ and $0\leq s_i\leq r_i$ for all $i$, and \item[] $\gcd(a-1,n)=2^{m''}p_1^{t_1}\cdots p_k^{t_k}$ with $m''\leq m$ and $0\leq t_i\leq r_i$ for all $i$. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Factor $n$ and write the prime factorizations of $\gcd(a\pm1,n)$.

nodes.name: Disjointness of prime factors
nodes.statement: Now, we note that for all $i\in\{1,...,k\}$ either $s_i=0$ or $t_i=0$. Indeed, if $s_i>0$ and $t_i>0$ then $p_i$ divides both $a-1$ and $a+1$ which is impossible (since $p_i>2$). Similarly, either $m'\leq1$ or $m''\leq1$; otherwise, $2^{\min\{m',m''\}}$ divides $a-1$ and $a+1$ which is impossible.
nodes.statement_short: For each odd prime, $a-1$ and $a+1$ cannot both be divisible; similarly $m'\le1$ or $m''\le1$.

nodes.name: Deduce $1\le j\le 2$
nodes.statement: Since $\gcd(a+1,n)\gcd(a-1,n)=jn$, we have that $$2^{m'+m''}p_1^{s_1+t_1}\cdots p_k^{s_k+t_k}=j2^mp_1^{r_1}\cdots p_k^{r_k}.$$ Now, since for all $i$ either $t_i=0$ or $s_i=0$, we necessarily have $s_i+t_i=r_i$. Dividing out, we get $2^{m'+m''}=j2^m$. We also know that $m'\leq m$ and $m''\leq m$ and since either $m'\leq 1$ or $m''\leq 1$, we have $m\leq m'+m''\leq m+1$. Dividing out we have $j=2^{m'+m''-m}$ and so $1\leq j\leq 2$ as required.
nodes.statement_short: Comparing exponents gives $j=2^{m'+m''-m}$ with $m\le m'+m''\le m+1$.

nodes.name: Claim (2) via Theorem 2.7
nodes.statement: Now, according to Theorem \ref{unorbits}, $N_a$ is the number of divisors of $\frac{\gcd(a-1,n)\gcd(a+1,n)}{n}$, and thus $N_a$ is the number of divisors of $j$ computed above. Therefore, $N_a=1$ if $j=1$ and $N_a=2$ if $j=2$. In either case, $N_a = |\zdiv{a+1}/\langle a-1 \rangle| \le 2$ proving Claim (2).
nodes.statement_short: Theorem 2.7 makes $N_a$ the number of divisors of $j$, so $N_a\le2$.

nodes.name: Claim (3)
nodes.statement: Finally, according to the proof of (1), we have $j=2$ if and only if $m'=1$ and $m''=m$ or $m'=m$ and $m''=1$. In the first case, we have that $2^m$ divides $a-1$, and in the second case we have that $2^m$ divides $a+1$. Therefore, $a \equiv \pm 1 \pmod{2^m}$.
nodes.statement_short: $j=2$ forces $2^m\mid a-1$ or $2^m\mid a+1$, i.e. $a\equiv\pm1\pmod{2^m}$.

nodes.name: Setup from Theorem 4.5
nodes.statement: According to Theorem \ref{thm:equivinvols}, we know $N_a$ for every $a\in\mathcal{R}_n^2$.
nodes.statement_short: Use the values of $N_a$ supplied by Theorem 4.5.

nodes.name: Case $m=0$
nodes.statement: When $m=0$, $n$ is odd and we know that $N_a=1$ for all $a$. Thus, there is one equivalence class for every element of $\mathcal{R}_n^2$ proving the first formula.
nodes.statement_short: For odd $n$ every $N_a=1$, giving $|\mathcal{R}_n^2|$ classes.

nodes.name: Case $m=1,2$
nodes.statement: If $m=1,2$, then every $a\in\mathcal{R}_n^2$ is odd and so satisfies $a\equiv \pm 1\pmod{m}$. Thus for every element $a\in\mathcal{R}_n^2$, we get two equivalence classes for a total of $2\cdot|\mathcal{R}_n^2|$ equivalence classes.
nodes.statement_short: Every $a$ satisfies the congruence, so each contributes two classes.

nodes.name: Case $m\geq3$
nodes.statement: Finally, when $m\geq 3$, using the construction of the elements of $\mathcal{R}_n^2$ found in the proof in the appendix, we see that exactly half of these elements satisfy the condition $a\equiv\pm 1\pmod{m}$. Therefore, for half the elements in $\mathcal{R}_n^2$ we have $N_a=1$ and for the other half we have $N_a=2$ giving us a total of $2^{k+2}+(2^{k+2}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot2^{k+2})=2^{k+3}-2^{k+1}$ equivalence classes, proving the result.
nodes.statement_short: Exactly half the square roots satisfy the congruence, giving $2^{k+3}-2^{k+1}$.

nodes.name: $\psi(Q)$ as a union of two cosets
nodes.statement: We proceed using Theorem \ref{thm:hqr} and applying Theorem \ref{thm:equivinvols}. Indeed, by Theorem \ref{thm:hqr} $\psi(Q)$ consists of the union of the two cosets $\langle a-1 \rangle$ and $-b + \langle a-1 \rangle$.
nodes.statement_short: By Theorem 3.1, $\psi(Q)=\langle a-1\rangle\cup(-b+\langle a-1\rangle)$.

nodes.name: Case: cosets coincide
nodes.statement: These cosets are the same if $-b \in \langle a-1 \rangle$ (which means $b\in\langle a-1\rangle$) and then $\psi(Q) = \langle a - 1 \rangle \le \zdiv{a+1}$,
nodes.statement_short: If $b\in\langle a-1\rangle$ the two cosets agree and $\psi(Q)=\langle a-1\rangle$.

nodes.name: Case: cosets distinct
nodes.statement: or they are distinct and by Theorem \ref{thm:equivinvols} part (1) there are only 2 cosets total so $\langle a - 1 \rangle \cup (-b+\langle a - 1 \rangle) = \zdiv{a+1}$. In either case, $Q$ is a subgroup of $\langle r \rangle$ and $\psi(Q)$ is as described in the statement of the corollary.
nodes.statement_short: Otherwise Theorem 4.5(1) leaves only two cosets, so their union is $\zdiv{a+1}$.

nodes.name: Description of $R\setminus Q$
nodes.statement: Finally, the result about $R \setminus Q$ is immediate from equation \eqref{eqn:R}.
nodes.statement_short: The formula for $R\setminus Q$ follows from equation (4.2).

nodes.name: Construct the counterexample
nodes.statement: Let $n=8$ and $\theta_1=7x$ and $\theta_2=3x$.
nodes.statement_short: Take $n=8$, $\theta_1=7x$, $\theta_2=3x$.

nodes.name: They are inequivalent
nodes.statement: According to Proposition \ref{prop:equivalence}, $\theta_1\not\sim\theta_2$ because $7 \ne 3$ (in $U_8$).
nodes.statement_short: Proposition 2.5 gives $\theta_1\not\sim\theta_2$ since $7\ne3$ in $U_8$.

nodes.name: Their fixed groups coincide
nodes.statement: However, according to Theorem \ref{thm:hqr}, $H_{\theta_1}=\{1, r^4, s, r^4s\}$ and $H_{\theta_2}=\{1, r^4, s, r^4s\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Theorem 3.1 gives $H_{\theta_1}=H_{\theta_2}=\{1,r^4,s,r^4s\}$.

nodes.name: Part (1)
nodes.statement: Part (1) follows from the equations \eqref{congruences} given in the proof of Proposition \ref{prop:orderk}.
nodes.statement_short: The congruences (2.1), read over $\Z$, force $\theta=-x+b$.

nodes.name: Part (2)
nodes.statement: For part (2), observe that Proposition \ref{prop:equivalence} holds for $D_\infty$ and says that $-x + b \sim -x + d$ if and only if either $b - d \in 2\Z$ or $-b-d \in 2\Z$, equivalently: $b \equiv d \pmod{2}$.
nodes.statement_short: Proposition 2.5 over $\Z$ gives $-x+b\sim-x+d$ iff $b\equiv d\pmod2$.

nodes.name: Goal
nodes.statement: Our goal is to determine the size of $|\mathcal{R}_n^2|$ for all $n$.
nodes.statement_short: State the goal: compute $|\mathcal{R}_n^2|$ for all $n$.

nodes.name: Odd prime powers
nodes.statement: First, suppose that $n=p^r$ where $p$ is an odd prime and $r\geq 1$. Then, suppose $a\in\Z_{p^r}$ and that $a^2-1\equiv 0\pmod{p^r}$. Then we have that $(a+1)(a-1)\equiv 0$ (mod $p^r$) and so $(a+1)(a-1)=kp^r$ for some $k\in\Z$. Since $p$ is an odd prime, it is clear that both $a+1$ and $a-1$ cannot divide $p^d$ for any $d\geq 1$ and so we have that $a+1=p^r$ or $a-1=p^r$. This implies that $a=1$ or $a=n-1$, thus $|\mathcal{R}_{p^r}^2|=2$.
nodes.statement_short: For odd prime powers only $a=\pm1$ are square roots, so $|\mathcal{R}_{p^r}^2|=2$.

nodes.name: Small $2$-powers
nodes.statement: Next, it is clear that $|\mathcal{R}_2^2|=1$ and $|\mathcal{R}_4^2|=2$.
nodes.statement_short: Record $|\mathcal{R}_2^2|=1$ and $|\mathcal{R}_4^2|=2$.

nodes.name: Set up the case $n=2^m$, $m\ge3$
nodes.statement: Suppose that $n=2^m$ with $m\geq 3$. Next, suppose that $a\in\Z_n\setminus\{1,n-1\}$ with $a^2\equiv 1$ (mod $n$). Since $n$ is even, we must have that $a$ is odd, so assume that $a=2k+1$ for some $0\leq k\leq 2^{m-1}$. Then $1\equiv a^2\equiv (2k+1)^2\equiv 4k^2+4k+1$ (mod $n$) so that $4k(k+1)=l\cdot 2^m$ for some $l\geq 1$. In particular, since $m\geq 3$, we have $k(k+1)=l\cdot 2^{m-2}$ for some $m$. Either $k$ or $k+1$ is odd and thus cannot divide $2^{m-2}$. \begin{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Write $a=2k+1$ and reduce $a^2\equiv1$ to $k(k+1)=l\cdot2^{m-2}$.

nodes.name: Case 1: $k$ even
nodes.statement: \item[] Case 1: $k$ is even. So $k=h\cdot 2^{m-2}$ for some $1\leq h\leq 2$ (since $k\leq 2^{m-1})$. Then, if $h=1$, $a=2^{m-1}+1$. If $h=2$, then $a\equiv 1$ (mod $n$).
nodes.statement_short: If $k$ is even then $a=2^{m-1}+1$ or $a\equiv1$.

nodes.name: Case 2: $k$ odd
nodes.statement: \item[] Case 2: $k$ is odd. So $k+1$ is even and $k+1=h\cdot 2^{m-2}$ with $1\leq h\leq 2$. Then, if $h=1$, $a=2^{m-1}-1$. If $h=2$, then $a=2^m-1\equiv n-1\equiv -1$ (mod $n$). \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: If $k$ is odd then $a=2^{m-1}-1$ or $a\equiv-1$.

nodes.name: Four square roots mod $2^m$
nodes.statement: So, there are four possibilities for $a$: $1,-1,2^{m-1}+1,2^{m-1}-1$. It is easy to check that these are all in fact square roots of 1, showing that $|\mathcal{R}_{2^m}^2|=4$ if $m\geq 3$.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude $|\mathcal{R}_{2^m}^2|=4$ for $m\ge3$.

nodes.name: Recombine by the Chinese Remainder Theorem
nodes.statement: Finally, the result holds due to the fact that the Chinese Remainder Theorem guarantees that if $n=2^mp_1^{r_1}\cdots p_k^{r_k}$ then $$\Z_n\cong \Z_{2^m}\times\Z_{p_1^{r_1}}\times\cdots\times \Z_{p_k^{r_k}}.$$ Then, it is clear that any square root of $(1,...,1)$ (the identity from the right hand side) must be of the form $(a_0,a_1,...,a_k)$ where $a_0\in\mathcal{R}_{2^m}^2$ and $a_i\in\mathcal{R}_{p_i^{r_i}}^n$ for $i\in\{1,...,k\}$. We have counted the possibilities for $a_i$ above and so we can multiply these together to get all the possible choices for $a\in\Z_n$ with $a^2\equiv 1$ (mod $n$). In particular, we get $|\mathcal{R}_n^2|=2^k$ if $m\in\{0,1\}$, $|\mathcal{R}_n^2|=2\cdot2^k$ if $m=2$ and $|\mathcal{R}_n^2|=2^2\cdot2^k$ if $m\geq 3$ as required.
nodes.statement_short: CRT multiplies the local counts to give the stated formula.
